why: Insert by the ordering, then find the LCA by the ordering. The insight: the LCA is the first inserted value lying between p and q, because until it arrives p and q always fall on the same side of every node.
hints: Build the tree by insertion and walk down from the root as in BST LCA. Then ask: is the tree even needed?
When a value v with min(p,q) <= v <= max(p,q) is inserted, p and q (inserted later or v itself) end up on different sides of v or equal to it, and every earlier node sends both the same way.
Either build the BST and do the split-point walk, or scan insertionOrder once and return the first value in [min(p,q), max(p,q)]. The scan is O(n) even when the tree degenerates into a chain.
pitfalls: Sorted insertion order turns the tree into a 100000-node chain: avoid recursion.
A node is its own ancestor.
